_link.title: I can explain how disruption to cell cycle regulation leads to cancer development

toLevel2.question: How does cancer develop in terms of DNA mutations?

options.text: Through a series of progressive DNA mutations that accumulate over time
options.explanation: Cancer develops through multiple mutations that progressively disable checkpoints and regulatory mechanisms.

options.text: Through a single mutation that immediately causes a malignant tumour
options.explanation: Cancer requires multiple mutations, not a single one; it is a multi-step process.

options.text: Through normal cell division that occurs without any mutations at all
options.explanation: Cancer involves DNA mutations that disrupt cell cycle regulation; it is not normal division.

options.text: Through the repair of damaged DNA by regulatory proteins
options.explanation: DNA repair prevents cancer; cancer develops when repair fails and mutations accumulate.

toLevel2.question: What happens when regulatory proteins like p53 are damaged?

options.text: They cannot detect errors, halt the cell cycle, or trigger apoptosis
options.explanation: Damaged p53 loses its ability to detect DNA errors, stop division, or initiate programmed cell death.

options.text: They become more effective at detecting and repairing damaged DNA
options.explanation: Damaged p53 loses function; it does not become more effective.

options.text: They speed up the cell cycle to replace damaged cells faster
options.explanation: Damaged p53 cannot regulate the cycle; it does not speed up replacement.

options.text: They have no effect on the cell cycle or cancer development
options.explanation: p53 damage has major consequences; it removes key checkpoint protection.

toLevel2.question: What is the difference between a benign tumour and a malignant tumour?

options.text: Benign tumours are localised; malignant tumours can invade tissue and metastasise
options.explanation: Benign tumours stay in one place, while malignant tumours can invade surrounding tissue and spread via the bloodstream.

options.text: Benign tumours are more dangerous than malignant tumours overall
options.explanation: Malignant tumours are more dangerous because they can invade and metastasise.

options.text: Both types of tumour behave identically and pose equal health risks
options.explanation: They differ significantly; malignant tumours can spread while benign ones remain localised.

options.text: Malignant tumours are always smaller than benign tumours in size
options.explanation: Size does not determine malignancy; the key difference is the ability to invade and spread.

toLevel2.question: Which of the following factors can contribute to the mutations that lead to cancer?

options.text: UV radiation, cigarette smoke, pollution, age, and genetic predisposition
options.explanation: Multiple factors contribute to mutation accumulation, including environmental, lifestyle, and genetic factors.

options.text: Only UV radiation causes the mutations that lead to cancer development
options.explanation: Many factors contribute, including cigarette smoke, pollution, age, and genetics.

options.text: Only genetic predisposition determines whether cancer will develop
options.explanation: Genetics is one factor; environmental factors like UV and smoking also contribute significantly.

options.text: No external factors contribute to cancer; it is entirely random
options.explanation: External factors like UV radiation and cigarette smoke are well-established contributors.

toLevel2.question: What is the multi-step nature of cancer development?

options.text: Multiple mutations accumulate: one increases division, another forms a tumour, another makes it malignant
options.explanation: Cancer progresses through stages as each new mutation adds another abnormal capability to the cells.

options.text: Cancer occurs in a single step when one mutation transforms a cell instantly
options.explanation: Cancer is a multi-step process requiring several mutations, not a single transformation.

options.text: All mutations occur simultaneously during one cell division event
options.explanation: Mutations accumulate over time through multiple cell divisions, not all at once.

options.text: Cancer requires exactly two mutations and no more to fully develop
options.explanation: Cancer typically requires multiple mutations, not just two; it is a progressive process.

toLevel2.question: Cancer develops through a single mutation that immediately causes uncontrolled cell division.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Cancer is a multi-step process requiring multiple progressive mutations, not a single one.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. Cancer develops through a series of progressive mutations that accumulate over time, not from a single event.

toLevel2.question: Factors like UV radiation, cigarette smoke, and genetic predisposition can all contribute to producing abnormal regulatory proteins that lead to cancer.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Multiple environmental and genetic factors can cause mutations in regulatory genes like p53, contributing to cancer development.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. UV radiation, smoking, and genetics are all recognised contributors to cancer-causing mutations.

options.explanation: Cancer arises from progressive DNA mutations that disable cell cycle controls.

options.explanation: Ribosomes are protein-making organelles; mutations help cells bypass checkpoints.

options.text: mitochondria
options.explanation: Mitochondria produce energy; mutations help cells bypass cell cycle checkpoints.

toLevel2.question: A benign tumour is {{blank:1}}, while a malignant tumour can invade tissue and {{blank:2}} through the bloodstream.

options.text: localised
options.explanation: Benign tumours remain at their original site and do not spread to other locations.

options.text: malignant
options.explanation: Malignant describes tumours that invade and spread; benign tumours are localised.

options.text: spreading
options.explanation: Spreading describes malignant tumours; benign tumours are localised.

options.text: metastasise
options.explanation: Malignant tumours can metastasise, spreading through the bloodstream to form secondary tumours.

options.text: differentiate
options.explanation: Differentiation is cells becoming specialised; metastasis is cancer spreading to new sites.

options.text: regenerate
options.explanation: Regeneration is tissue repair; metastasis is the spread of cancer cells.

toLevel3.question: Why is cancer described as a multi-step process rather than a single-event disease?

options.text: Multiple mutations must accumulate to disable different regulatory mechanisms before cancer fully develops
options.explanation: Each mutation removes another layer of protection; cancer requires the failure of multiple safeguards.

options.text: Cancer always occurs instantly when a cell is first exposed to a mutagen
options.explanation: Cancer requires multiple mutations over time, not a single exposure event.

options.text: Only one mutation is needed but it takes many years for the cell to respond
options.explanation: Multiple distinct mutations are needed, not just time for one mutation to take effect.

options.text: The term 'multi-step' refers to the treatment process, not cancer development
options.explanation: Multi-step refers to the progressive accumulation of mutations during cancer development.

toLevel3.question: Explain how UV radiation can contribute to cancer development through its effect on p53.

options.text: UV damages the p53 gene, producing an abnormal protein that cannot halt the cycle or trigger apoptosis
options.explanation: UV-induced mutations in p53 disable its checkpoint functions, allowing damaged cells to continue dividing.

options.text: UV radiation strengthens p53, making it more effective at preventing cancer
options.explanation: UV damages p53; it does not strengthen it. Damaged p53 increases cancer risk.

options.text: UV radiation has no effect on DNA or regulatory proteins in any cell
options.explanation: UV radiation is a well-known mutagen that can damage DNA and regulatory genes like p53.

options.text: UV radiation only affects skin colour and does not contribute to cancer risk
options.explanation: UV radiation causes DNA mutations that can damage p53 and increase cancer risk.

toLevel3.question: Why does the accumulation of mutations over time explain why cancer is more common in older people?

options.text: Older cells have had more time to accumulate the multiple mutations needed for cancer to develop
options.explanation: With more cell divisions and more exposure to mutagens over a lifetime, the chance of accumulating enough mutations increases.

options.text: Older people have weaker immune systems that directly cause all cancer mutations
options.explanation: While immunity declines, the primary reason is the accumulation of mutations over time.

options.text: Cancer mutations only begin occurring after a person reaches a certain age threshold
options.explanation: Mutations can occur at any age; they accumulate progressively over a lifetime.

options.text: Age has no connection to cancer risk because mutations are entirely random events
options.explanation: Age increases cancer risk because mutations accumulate with time and exposure.

toLevel3.question: How does the failure of checkpoint proteins contribute to the progression from a benign to a malignant tumour?

options.text: Without checkpoints, cells accumulate further mutations that give them invasive and metastatic abilities
options.explanation: Each checkpoint failure allows more mutations to pass unchecked, eventually enabling invasion and metastasis.

options.text: Checkpoint proteins directly cause tumours to become malignant when they function normally
options.explanation: Normal checkpoint proteins prevent cancer; their failure allows progression to malignancy.

options.text: Benign tumours cannot become malignant regardless of checkpoint protein status
options.explanation: Benign tumours can become malignant through additional mutations, especially when checkpoints fail.

options.text: Checkpoint failure only affects cell size, not the tumour's ability to spread at all
options.explanation: Checkpoint failure allows accumulation of mutations that enable invasion and metastasis.

toLevel3.question: Why do multiple factors (UV, smoking, genetics) all contribute to cancer risk?

options.text: Each factor can cause DNA mutations that contribute to the progressive accumulation needed for cancer
options.explanation: Different mutagens and genetic factors all add to the total mutation load, increasing the chance of disabling critical regulatory genes.

options.text: Only one of these factors actually causes cancer; the others are unrelated
options.explanation: Multiple factors are established cancer risk contributors; they all cause or contribute to mutations.

options.text: These factors only affect cells temporarily and do not cause lasting DNA changes
options.explanation: These factors cause permanent DNA mutations that accumulate and increase cancer risk.

options.text: All these factors must be present simultaneously for cancer to develop at all
options.explanation: Any combination of these factors can contribute; they do not all need to be present.

toLevel3.question: Explain why the loss of apoptosis is a critical step in cancer development.

options.text: Without apoptosis, cells with damaged DNA survive and continue dividing instead of being destroyed
options.explanation: Apoptosis is the last line of defence; without it, cells with irreparable damage persist and accumulate more mutations.

options.text: Apoptosis promotes cancer by killing healthy cells and leaving damaged ones behind
options.explanation: Apoptosis targets damaged cells; its loss allows damaged cells to survive.

options.text: The loss of apoptosis has no effect on cancer because cell death is not related to tumour growth
options.explanation: Apoptosis is critical for removing damaged cells; its loss is directly linked to cancer progression.

options.text: Apoptosis only removes old cells and has no role in preventing cancer from developing
options.explanation: Apoptosis removes damaged cells that could become cancerous; its loss increases cancer risk.

toLevel3.question: A benign tumour can potentially become malignant if additional mutations give the cells the ability to invade tissue and metastasise.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. Further mutations can transform a benign tumour into a malignant one by enabling invasion and metastasis.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Benign tumours can progress to malignancy through additional mutations.

toLevel4.question: A patient who has smoked for 30 years develops lung cancer. Apply the multi-step model of cancer to explain this outcome.

options.text: Decades of smoke exposure caused progressive mutations that eventually disabled enough checkpoints for cancer to develop
options.explanation: Chronic exposure to cigarette smoke causes ongoing DNA damage, with mutations accumulating over years until regulatory systems fail.

options.text: A single cigarette caused the cancer mutation that appeared 30 years later
options.explanation: Cancer is multi-step; decades of exposure caused progressive mutation accumulation, not a single event.

options.text: The cancer is unrelated to smoking because lung cancer is always genetic
options.explanation: Smoking is a major environmental contributor to lung cancer through DNA mutation accumulation.

options.text: The cancer developed immediately but took 30 years to be detected by medical tests
options.explanation: Cancer develops progressively through mutation accumulation, not instantly with delayed detection.

toLevel4.question: A researcher discovers a new chemical that causes mutations in checkpoint genes. Predict the long-term consequence of exposure to this chemical.

options.text: Increased cancer risk because damaged checkpoints would allow cells with errors to divide
options.explanation: Mutations in checkpoint genes disable the regulatory system, allowing damaged cells to divide and accumulate further mutations.

options.text: Decreased cancer risk because the mutations would strengthen checkpoint function
options.explanation: Mutations in checkpoint genes typically disable them, increasing cancer risk.

options.text: No change in cancer risk because chemicals cannot cause DNA mutations
options.explanation: Many chemicals are mutagens that can damage DNA; mutations in checkpoint genes increase cancer risk.

options.text: Immediate cancer development after a single exposure to the chemical
options.explanation: Cancer requires multiple mutations; a single exposure increases risk but does not cause immediate cancer.

toLevel4.question: Two siblings inherit one faulty copy of the p53 gene. One develops cancer at age 25, the other at age 50. Apply the multi-step model to explain the difference.

options.text: The sibling who developed cancer earlier accumulated the remaining needed mutations faster due to additional exposures
options.explanation: Starting with one faulty p53 copy, additional mutations are needed; different exposure levels explain the timing difference.

options.text: The inherited p53 mutation only affects one sibling and not the other at all
options.explanation: Both inherited the same mutation; the difference is in when additional mutations accumulate.

options.text: Age has no effect on when cancer develops in people with inherited mutations
options.explanation: Additional environmental and random mutations accumulate at different rates, affecting timing.

options.text: The sibling at age 50 does not actually have the p53 mutation despite inheriting it
options.explanation: Both have the inherited mutation; the timing difference reflects different rates of additional mutation accumulation.

toLevel4.question: A doctor explains to a patient that their benign tumour has a chance of becoming malignant over time. Apply your knowledge to explain why monitoring is important.

options.text: Additional mutations could give the tumour cells invasive and metastatic abilities, so early detection is crucial
options.explanation: Benign tumours can progress to malignancy through further mutations; monitoring allows early intervention.

options.text: Benign tumours always become malignant so monitoring is unnecessary since the outcome is certain
options.explanation: Not all benign tumours become malignant; monitoring tracks whether dangerous changes occur.

options.text: Benign tumours can never become malignant so monitoring is a waste of resources
options.explanation: Benign tumours can become malignant through additional mutations; monitoring is important.

options.text: Monitoring has no medical benefit because cancer cannot be prevented or treated at all
options.explanation: Early detection through monitoring significantly improves treatment outcomes.

toLevel4.question: A person with a genetic predisposition to cancer asks what lifestyle changes could reduce their risk. Apply the multi-step model to provide advice.

options.text: Reducing exposure to mutagens like UV and cigarette smoke slows the accumulation of additional mutations needed for cancer
options.explanation: Since cancer requires multiple mutations, reducing exposure to mutagens decreases the rate of mutation accumulation.

options.text: Lifestyle changes have no effect because genetic predisposition guarantees cancer development
options.explanation: Genetic predisposition increases risk but does not guarantee cancer; reducing mutagen exposure helps.

options.text: They should increase sun exposure to strengthen their cells against future mutations
options.explanation: UV radiation causes DNA mutations; increasing exposure would increase cancer risk.

options.text: Only medical treatment can affect cancer risk; lifestyle has no influence on mutations
options.explanation: Lifestyle choices directly affect mutagen exposure and mutation accumulation rates.

toLevel4.question: A cell has lost p53 function but has not yet formed a tumour. Predict what must happen next for cancer to develop.

options.text: Additional mutations must accumulate to increase division rate and eventually enable invasion and metastasis
options.explanation: Loss of p53 is one step; further mutations are needed to drive uncontrolled growth and malignancy.

options.text: The cell will immediately form a malignant tumour without any further mutations needed
options.explanation: Cancer is multi-step; loss of p53 alone is not sufficient for full malignant transformation.

options.text: The cell will repair its p53 gene automatically and return to normal function
options.explanation: Once p53 is mutated, the cell cannot automatically repair it; further mutations are likely.

options.text: Nothing further needs to happen because p53 loss is the only required step for cancer
options.explanation: Multiple mutations are needed; p53 loss removes one layer of protection but others must also fail.

toLevel4.question: A public health campaign warns about the combined effects of smoking and UV exposure on cancer risk. Apply the multi-step model to explain why combining risk factors is especially dangerous.

options.text: Multiple mutagens increase the rate of mutation accumulation, reaching the cancer threshold faster
options.explanation: Each mutagen independently contributes mutations; combining them accelerates the accumulation of damage needed for cancer.

options.text: Combining risk factors actually reduces cancer risk because the mutagens neutralise each other
options.explanation: Mutagens do not cancel each other; they add to the total mutation burden.

options.text: Only one risk factor matters; additional factors have no additive effect on cancer risk
options.explanation: Each risk factor contributes independently to mutation accumulation; their effects combine.

options.text: Combined exposure only matters if both mutagens target the exact same gene simultaneously
options.explanation: Different mutations in different genes all contribute to the multi-step cancer process.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why cancer is considered a disease of accumulated mutations rather than a single genetic defect.

options.text: Multiple independent regulatory mechanisms must fail before a cell can divide uncontrollably and become invasive
options.explanation: The body has multiple layers of protection (checkpoints, repair, apoptosis); cancer requires the failure of several, which needs multiple mutations.

options.text: A single mutation in any gene is sufficient to cause full malignant cancer immediately
options.explanation: Cancer requires multiple mutations affecting different protective mechanisms, not a single gene defect.

options.text: All mutations in cancer affect the same gene and simply make it progressively worse
options.explanation: Cancer mutations typically affect multiple different genes, each disabling a different protective mechanism.

options.text: Mutations do not actually cause cancer; it is entirely determined by environmental factors alone
options.explanation: Environmental factors cause mutations in DNA; it is these accumulated mutations that drive cancer development.

toLevel5.question: Analyse the relationship between genetic predisposition and environmental mutagen exposure in determining cancer risk.

options.text: Genetic predisposition provides some mutations from birth, so fewer additional environmental mutations are needed to reach the cancer threshold
options.explanation: Inherited mutations give a head start toward cancer; fewer environmental hits are needed to disable remaining protective mechanisms.

options.text: Genetic predisposition and environment are completely independent with no interaction between them
options.explanation: They interact: inherited mutations reduce the number of additional environmental mutations needed for cancer.

options.text: Environmental factors only matter if there is no genetic predisposition present at all
options.explanation: Environmental factors contribute to cancer in everyone; genetic predisposition increases vulnerability but is not required.

options.text: Genetic predisposition makes a person immune to environmental mutagen effects on their cells
options.explanation: Genetic predisposition increases vulnerability; it does not provide immunity to mutagens.

toLevel5.question: Compare how the multi-step model of cancer explains why some people who smoke heavily never develop cancer while others develop it from minimal exposure.

options.text: Individual genetic makeup affects how many inherited mutations are present and how effectively DNA repair mechanisms work
options.explanation: Genetic variation in repair efficiency and inherited mutation load means different people reach the cancer threshold at different exposure levels.

options.text: Smoking has no connection to cancer and the outcomes are entirely random in all cases
options.explanation: Smoking is a proven cancer cause; individual variation in response is explained by genetic differences.

options.text: Everyone who smokes will eventually develop cancer given enough time and exposure
options.explanation: Not everyone who smokes develops cancer; genetic factors influence individual vulnerability.

options.text: The multi-step model cannot explain individual variation in cancer risk between people
options.explanation: The model explains variation through differences in inherited mutations and repair capacity.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why targeting multiple cancer mechanisms simultaneously (e.g., restoring checkpoints and apoptosis) is more effective than targeting just one.

options.text: Cancer involves multiple disabled mechanisms, so restoring several layers of protection provides more comprehensive control
options.explanation: Since cancer disables multiple safeguards, restoring several mechanisms closes more gaps in the cell's protective systems.

options.text: Targeting one mechanism is always sufficient because cancer only involves one faulty pathway
options.explanation: Cancer involves multiple faulty pathways; targeting only one leaves other escape routes for cancer cells.

options.text: Targeting multiple mechanisms is less effective because the treatments interfere with each other
options.explanation: Combination approaches are generally more effective because they address multiple aspects of cancer.

options.text: Cancer treatment never involves restoring cell cycle mechanisms in any clinical approach
options.explanation: Many cancer therapies aim to restore or mimic normal cell cycle control mechanisms.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the transition from benign to malignant is considered the most critical step in cancer progression.

options.text: Malignancy enables invasion and metastasis, spreading cancer throughout the body and making treatment much harder
options.explanation: While benign tumours are localised and often treatable, malignant transformation allows spread, dramatically worsening prognosis.

options.text: Benign tumours are more dangerous than malignant ones so this transition is actually beneficial
options.explanation: Malignant tumours are more dangerous; the transition increases threat due to invasion and metastasis.

options.text: The transition has no clinical significance because treatment is identical for both tumour types
options.explanation: Treatment differs dramatically; malignant tumours require more aggressive, systemic treatment.

options.text: All benign tumours are guaranteed to become malignant so the transition is inevitable
options.explanation: Not all benign tumours become malignant; the transition requires additional specific mutations.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why cancer prevention strategies focus on reducing mutagen exposure rather than eliminating all mutations.

options.text: Eliminating all mutations is impossible since they occur naturally, but reducing mutagen exposure slows their accumulation
options.explanation: Some mutations occur during normal DNA replication; prevention focuses on reducing preventable, mutagen-caused additions to the mutation load.

options.text: All mutations can be prevented through medication so mutagen reduction is unnecessary
options.explanation: Spontaneous mutations cannot be prevented; reducing mutagen exposure is the practical approach.

options.text: Mutations do not contribute to cancer so reducing exposure to mutagens serves no purpose
options.explanation: Mutations are the direct cause of cancer; reducing mutagen exposure reduces the rate of mutation accumulation.

options.text: Prevention strategies only target genetic predisposition and ignore environmental factors entirely
options.explanation: Prevention strategies primarily target reducible environmental exposures like UV and smoking.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why different types of cancer (lung, skin, liver) can all result from the same fundamental process of checkpoint failure and mutation accumulation.

options.text: All cell types use the same checkpoint system, so mutations disrupting it can cause cancer in any tissue
options.explanation: The cell cycle and its checkpoints are universal in all dividing cells; disrupting them can cause cancer in any tissue type.

options.text: Different cancers are caused by completely different mechanisms with no common features
options.explanation: All cancers share the common feature of checkpoint failure and mutation accumulation.

options.text: Only one type of tissue can develop cancer; others are immune to mutation effects
options.explanation: Any dividing tissue can develop cancer through mutation accumulation and checkpoint failure.

options.text: The checkpoint system only operates in skin cells and is absent from internal organs
options.explanation: The checkpoint system operates in all dividing cells, not just skin cells.

toLevel5.question: Analyse the implications of the multi-step model for cancer screening and early detection programs.

options.text: Early detection catches tumours at the benign stage before additional mutations enable malignancy and metastasis
options.explanation: Screening can detect tumours before they acquire the mutations needed for invasion and spread, improving treatment success.

options.text: Screening is pointless because cancer either develops or it does not, regardless of detection timing
options.explanation: Early detection allows treatment before malignant transformation, significantly improving outcomes.

options.text: Cancer always develops too quickly for screening to detect it at any treatable stage
options.explanation: Cancer develops over years through progressive mutations; screening can catch it at earlier stages.

options.text: The multi-step model has no relevance to screening because mutations occur all at once
options.explanation: The gradual nature of cancer development is exactly why screening is effective.
